intro:
John writes 2 John around same time as 1 John (AD 85-95) to 'the chosen lady and her children'—likely a coded reference to a local church and its members. This shortest New Testament book addresses hospitality: should churches welcome traveling teachers who deny Jesus came in flesh?

The situation mirrors 1 John: deceivers have gone out into world, denying incarnation. These itinerant preachers depend on Christian hospitality for survival. John gives clear command: don't welcome or give any encouragement to those who bring false teaching about Christ. To do so shares in their wicked work.

This harsh-sounding instruction comes with balancing emphasis: 'love one another' (mentioned four times in 13 verses). True love protects the community from spiritual poison. John writes with pastoral urgency—he has more to say but hopes to visit soon to speak face-to-face 'so our joy may be complete.'

The letter shows early church grappling with boundaries: how to maintain unity without compromising truth. John's solution: radical hospitality toward true believers, radical exclusion toward those undermining gospel foundations.
outro:
John concludes with greetings from 'the children of your chosen sister'—likely another church. The emphasis on joy in fellowship underscores that truth and love aren't opposed but inseparable.

2 John became important for church discipline and boundary-setting. Its principle—don't extend Christian fellowship to those who deny core truths—guided early church responses to heresy. The balance between welcoming strangers (Hebrews 13:2) and testing spirits (1 John 4:1) remains challenging.

This brief letter demonstrates that love sometimes requires saying 'no.' Written when house churches networked across regions, it shows how shared doctrine enabled authentic community. The connection between truth and hospitality continues to shape how churches relate to teachers, missionaries, and one another.
